Some reactions are over in a flash and others take years, and one simple model explains every way you can speed one up or slow it down.

## Engage: hotter and faster?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Students' reasons for 'faster' (particles want to react, get bigger) surface here; the board's collision count replaces them with frequency and energy."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "A reaction takes 30 seconds at room temperature. You heat it by 100 °C. How long do you predict it takes?"
  options: ["About the same", "A little faster, maybe 25 seconds", "Much faster, a few seconds", "Slower"]
  actual: "Much faster. Particles move faster, so they collide more often and, more importantly, far more of the collisions have enough energy to react."
```

## Explore: two temperatures

```step
stage: run
insight: "Comparing times and the percentage of collisions that react shows energy, not just frequency, driving the change."
try: { playground: science, starter: "boards.yml#compare", height: 600 }
check: { type: board, text: "Run the reaction at two different temperatures and compare.", expect: { done: true } }
hint: ["Do one run, then change only the temperature before you run it again, so you know that's what made the difference.", "Move the temperature slider first and then press Reset, because a run only counts if the temperature stays the same from start to finish."]
```

Run it at 300 K first. Then move the temperature (try 500 K), press **Reset** so the new run starts clean, and run it again. Watch two numbers in the panel: **collisions** and **reactions**.

## Explain: collisions and energy

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Separating 'how often' from 'how hard' is the model; every rate factor is one or both."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Most collisions on the board did not make a reaction. Why not?"
      options: ["They didn't have enough energy: they were below the activation energy", "The particles were the wrong colour", "Only the first collision of each particle counts", "The particles were too far apart"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Colour is just a code for atom type.", "Particles can collide many times before one collision reacts.", "They touched: that is what a collision is."]
      explain: "A collision reacts only if it has at least the activation energy. The rest bounce off."
    hint: "Compare the collisions and reactions numbers in the panel: what was different about the few collisions that did react?"
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: "What happens when the temperature goes up?"
      options: ["True", "False"]
      items:
        - ["Particles move faster", "True"]
        - ["Collisions happen more often", "True"]
        - ["A larger share of collisions has enough energy", "True", "This is the bigger effect: see the percentage in the panel."]
        - ["Particles get bigger", "False", "Particles never change size."]
        - ["The activation energy gets smaller", "False", "The energy needed stays the same; more collisions reach it."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "A 100 °C rise doesn't make the particles collide 10 times more often, yet the reaction can go 10 times faster. What explains the rest?"
      options: ["Many more collisions have enough energy to react", "The particles stick together for longer", "The container gets bigger"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Particles bounce or react on contact; they don't linger.", "The container stays the same size."]
      explain: "Temperature changes how hard particles hit far more than how often. That is why heat has such a big effect."
    hint: "When you heated it on the board, what changed more: how many collisions there were, or the share of them that reacted?"
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "You want to test how temperature changes the rate of marble chips reacting with acid. Which plan is a fair test?"
      options: ["Change only the temperature, keep the acid and the chips the same, time the fizzing, and repeat each temperature", "Heat the acid and use stronger acid too, so the difference is bigger", "Do one run at each temperature: one result is enough"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Then you can't tell which change made it faster: change only one thing.", "Runs vary, as they did on the board: repeat each temperature and compare averages."]
      explain: "Change one factor, measure the rate (time until the fizzing stops, or gas made each minute) and keep everything else the same. Repeats show how much the results vary."
  - check:
      type: match
      q: "Each change speeds up a reaction. Match it to the reason, in collision terms."
      pairs:
        - ["Higher temperature", "Particles move faster: they collide more often and more of the collisions have enough energy"]
        - ["Higher concentration", "More reacting particles in the same space, so they collide more often"]
        - ["Larger surface area (smaller pieces)", "More particles of the solid are exposed, so more collisions can happen at once"]
        - ["A catalyst", "It lowers the activation energy, so a larger share of collisions succeed"]
      explain: "Every factor works through collisions: either more of them each second, or a bigger share with enough energy."
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "I explained, using collisions and activation energy, why heating makes a reaction faster." }
```

## Elaborate: concentration

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
insight: "Changing only the number of particles isolates collision frequency: the same share of collisions reacts, but there are more of them."
try: { playground: science, starter: "boards.yml#dilute", height: 580 }
tasks:
  - starter: "boards.yml#dilute"
    check: { type: board, text: "Run the low-concentration reaction to the target.", expect: { done: true } }
  - starter: "boards.yml#concentrated"
    check: { type: board, text: "Run the high-concentration reaction to the same target.", expect: { done: true } }
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "The concentrated reaction reached the target faster. Why?"
      options: ["More particles in the same space collide more often", "Each collision had more energy", "The activation energy was lower"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Same temperature, so the same energies: compare the percentage of collisions that react on the two boards.", "Same reaction, same activation energy."]
      explain: "Concentration changes how often particles collide, not how hard."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "A lump of chalk reacts slowly with acid; chalk powder fizzes fast. Which explanation fits collision theory?"
      options: ["Powder exposes far more particles to the acid, so there are more collisions each second", "Powder particles have more energy", "Powder is a different substance"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Same temperature, same energy. The difference is how many particles can be hit.", "It is the same chalk, in smaller pieces."]
      explain: "Surface area, like concentration, changes collision frequency."
```

## Elaborate: a catalyst

```step
stage: modify
tier: wider
insight: "A catalyst changes the threshold, not the particles' energy; comparing with heating shows two different routes to more successful collisions."
try: { playground: science, starter: "boards.yml#catalyst", height: 580 }
tasks:
  - check: { type: board, text: "Compare the reaction with and without the catalyst.", expect: { done: true } }
    hint: ["Do one run with the catalyst off, then turn it on and run it again with everything else the same.", "Press the Catalyst button first and then Reset, because a run only counts if nothing changes while it's going."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "With the catalyst, the reaction sped up but the temperature didn't change. How?"
      options: ["The catalyst lowered the activation energy, so more collisions had enough energy", "The catalyst gave the particles extra energy", "The catalyst reacted and was used up"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "The temperature in the panel didn't change, so the particles' energies didn't either.", "A catalyst is not a reactant: it may join in along the way, but it is given back unchanged, so the same amount is there at the end."]
      explain: "A catalyst provides a route with a lower activation energy. (In the model it simply halves the threshold; real catalysts often work on their surface.)"
    hint: "Did the temperature in the panel change when you turned the catalyst on, and what does that tell you about the particles' energy?"
```

## Evaluate: look back

```step
stage: info
check: { type: reflect, text: "I compared my prediction about heating with the results, and can explain any difference." }
```

Write one sentence: "At first I thought… Now I think… because…"

**Revision summary**

- Particles react only when they **collide** with at least the **activation energy**. Most collisions just bounce.
- **Temperature:** faster particles collide more often and, much more importantly, harder.
- **Concentration** and **surface area:** more collisions each second.
- **Catalyst:** a lower activation energy, so more collisions succeed. It is not used up.

```teacher
summary: Students explain reaction rate with collision theory (collisions with
  at least the activation energy) and use it to explain temperature,
  concentration, surface area and catalysts (AC9S10U07, node 5, a hinge node).
time: 30
timing: Engage and Explore 10 min · Explain 8 min · Evaluate 3 min · Typical
  adds 8 min, Wider about 5 min
goals:
  - I can explain that particles react only when they collide with at least the
    activation energy.
  - I can explain why more frequent or more energetic collisions make a reaction
    faster.
  - I can name and explain at least two ways to increase the rate.
before: >
  A concept tutorial for introducing or revising the idea; it does not replace a
  rate practical. Set the width with `?width=minimum`, `typical` (default) or
  `wider`.


  The hinge risk is rate factors learned as separate rules. Every factor answers
  one question: does it change how often particles collide, how hard, or the
  energy needed?


  Model notes: with 15 of each reactant, run times vary from run to run (often
  by a factor of two), as in real small-scale experiments. Use the class's runs
  together, or run twice at each temperature. Typical results at 300 K: 10–30 s;
  at 500 K: 3–5 s. The catalyst halves the activation energy for every
  collision.
running:
  - "Engage: record the class's predictions on the board to come back to."
  - "Explore: ask students to read out the percentage of collisions that react
    at each temperature. That number is the key to the Explain step."
  - "Explain: the third question separates frequency from energy; take it
    slowly."
  - "Typical: pool the class's two times on the board: the spread is part of the
    lesson."
struggle: "Explaining a rate change by how often particles collide and how many
  have enough energy. When a student says heat makes particles want to react,
  ask what changed in the panel: collisions, or the share that react."
stuck:
  - see: A student says heat makes the particles want to react.
    ask: "What changed in the panel: the number of collisions, or the share that
      react?"
    fix: "Both, but mostly the share: faster particles hit harder, so more
      collisions have the activation energy."
  - see: A student says every collision causes a reaction.
    ask: Compare the collisions and reactions numbers in the panel.
    fix: Only a few per cent react. The rest don't have enough energy.
  - see: A student says a catalyst adds energy.
    ask: Did the temperature change when you turned the catalyst on?
    fix: No. The catalyst lowers the energy needed instead.
stretch: Food in a freezer lasts months. Use collision theory to explain why,
  and why it still goes off eventually.
support: "Give a two-column frame for each factor: 'More collisions?' and 'More
  energetic collisions?'."
leads: >
  Next: rate factors investigated in practicals (node 6).


  In class: sodium thiosulfate and acid at different temperatures (the
  disappearing cross), or antacid tablets in water at different temperatures and
  as powder.
exit:
  q: Why does crushing a tablet make it dissolve and react faster in water?
  a: Crushing increases the surface area, so more particles are exposed and
    collisions happen more often.
explain: >
  Particles react only when they **collide** with at least the **activation
  energy**.


  - **Temperature:** particles collide more often and harder (the biggest
  effect).

  - **Concentration** and **surface area:** more collisions each second.

  - **Catalyst:** lowers the activation energy; not used up.
```
